title: Citizen suits and private enforcement
summary: Some regulatory statutes authorize injured citizens to enforce legal requirements, while preserving Article III and specified roles for public enforcement.
notes:
A citizen-suit provision gives specified private claimants a statutory route to enforce regulatory law. Under the Clean Water Act provision described in Laidlaw, a person with an adversely affected interest must provide advance notice, and diligent prosecution by EPA or the state can bar a citizen suit. Courts can award injunctions and civil penalties payable to the Treasury. The claimant still needs constitutional standing for each remedy.

Laidlaw supports penalties where their deterrent effect is likely to reduce the claimant’s exposure to ongoing or future violations. It distinguishes suits seeking only to punish wholly past violations. Its treatment of the state settlement also matters: the district court found that a prosecution arranged with assistance from Laidlaw had not been diligent enough to bar the private suit.

The opinions debate separation of powers. Justice Scalia argues that private penalty suits can displace executive enforcement judgment and confer disproportionate bargaining power. The majority emphasizes the deterrent relationship to concrete injury and the government’s statutory capacity to prosecute or intervene. Kennedy’s concurrence expressly reserves that issue.
